rows: Suspected measles requires urgent notification and public-health assessment.
Oral-fluid testing is recommended for suspected cases through the national pathway.
Case management considers symptoms, onset, infectious period and vaccination history.
Contacts should be identified according to exposure and timing.
Vulnerable contacts may require prompt post-exposure assessment.
MMR vaccination is central to prevention and outbreak control.
Healthcare, education and travel settings require setting-specific actions.
Clusters and outbreaks require coordinated epidemiological and laboratory investigation.
A rash, travel history or contact list does not establish measles or transmission.
Conclusions require clinical features, testing, timing, vaccination, exposure and UKHSA assessment.
Suspected, linked and confirmed pertussis cases can require public-health action.
Cases and contacts should be assessed using current national guidance.
Infants are at greatest risk of severe disease.
Antibiotics may reduce onward transmission when given within the recommended period.
Priority action focuses on people at high risk and those who may transmit to vulnerable infants.
Healthcare and educational clusters require setting-specific management.
Vaccination history should be reviewed for cases and contacts.
Surveillance and laboratory information support case and outbreak management.
A prolonged cough or contact with an infant does not establish pertussis.
Decisions require symptoms, timing, testing, vaccination, exposure, vulnerability and public-health evidence.
Mumps is a vaccine-preventable viral infection.
Oral-fluid testing can help confirm notified cases.
MMR vaccination is the principal preventive measure.
Case assessment should consider parotid swelling, timing and vaccination history.
Close-contact and setting advice depends on the circumstances of exposure.
Universities and other communal settings can experience outbreaks.
Outbreak response combines case finding, communication and vaccination review.
Parotid swelling or a university cluster does not establish mumps in each person.
Conclusions require clinical features, oral-fluid or laboratory evidence, timing, vaccination and epidemiological linkage.
Rubella is a vaccine-preventable viral infection.
Rubella infection during pregnancy can have serious fetal consequences.
Suspected cases require appropriate notification and laboratory confirmation.
Oral-fluid testing supports surveillance of notified cases.
MMR vaccination is used to prevent rubella.
Pregnancy status and exposure timing are important in risk assessment.
Contacts may require advice based on susceptibility and circumstances.
Cases and clusters should be managed with specialist public-health input.
A mild rash or pregnancy exposure does not establish rubella infection.
Conclusions require clinical, laboratory, timing, pregnancy, vaccination and exposure evidence.
